item.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners
item.description: The DOJ's embrace of fair use for AI training breaks with the White House's own framework, as OpenAI, Microsoft and news groups battle over copyright.
item.content:encoded:
One of the biggest court battles over artificial intelligence (AI) is putting an age-old legal principle to the test — and raising important questions about the Trump administration's AI policy.

Several news organizations, including The New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft for using millions of newspaper articles to train AI systems. The newspapers argue that the tech firms violated basic copyright protections. The tech firms contend that training their models on those articles qualifies as "fair use," a longstanding principle that allows copyrighted material to be used in certain ways without permission from or compensation to the copyright owner.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sided squarely with OpenAI's position — breaking with the administration's previously more balanced stance on the issue. The DOJ filed a statement of interest embracing an extreme vision of fair use that would grant AI companies virtually unfettered access to copyrighted material for commercial training, without obtaining permission from or compensating the creators whose works fuel these systems.

MIKE DAVIS: THE TRUMP DOJ SHOULD WITHDRAW ITS STATEMENT OF INTEREST IN THE OPENAI LAWSUIT

This expansive interpretation threatens to turn a narrow copyright exception into a blanket exemption for the world's most powerful and profitable industries.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

Those concerns deserve consideration. But the DOJ's aggressive arguments in the brief depart from more measured guidance elsewhere in the administration. The White House's official AI framework acknowledges valid arguments on both sides of the copyright debate.

Likewise, the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, adopted by G20 ministers at the Commerce Department's recent Innovation Ministerial, recognize that the intersection of AI and copyright poses "complex legal and policy questions." The principles note the "essential role" of copyright protections in supporting creators and call for respecting IP as a pillar of G20 AI policy.

MUSIC INDUSTRY FENDS OFF FLOOD OF AI MUSIC 'STEALING' THE CHARTS

The DOJ statement also overlooks how its stance could favor larger AI companies over smaller firms and startups. Several AI startups have argued that paying for the material they use provides more reliable access to training material, reduces legal uncertainty and improves models. Other companies have emerged to aggregate copyrights and make licensing easier.

It's particularly problematic for large AI companies to complain about paying for access to copyrighted materials. They are among the best positioned to pay for those materials, and doing so would help develop the kind of licensing markets they claim are lacking.

OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION

And even if national security were a legitimate justification, the government could not simply disregard property rights. The Constitution and other laws require just compensation when private property is taken for public use, and intellectual property rights are still property rights. Letting AI firms appropriate creators' IP without permission or compensation would be akin to letting data center builders seize private land without paying fair value.

If courts adopt the DOJ's position that fair use protects AI developers in virtually all circumstances, it would reduce incentives to create new works. Copyrights encourage creative work by assuring writers, artists and other creators that their work can't be easily stolen or copied. Licensing those rights allows creators to earn a living and underpins over $1 trillion in U.S. economic activity.

Weaker copyrights could result in fewer human-created books, articles, research papers, films and songs. Ironically, that could eventually leave AI systems with fewer and lower-quality materials to train on – a scenario that serves no one's interests.

All of this is why the Trump administration would be wise to follow its own AI framework and let the court system evaluate AI copyright disputes case by case, rather than arguing for unfettered fair use exceptions.

Policymakers also have a role to play. One promising bill is the bipartisan CLEAR Act. Introduced in February by California Democrat Sen. Adam Schiff and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, the CLEAR Act would require AI developers to publicly disclose the copyrighted works used in each new generative-AI model's training dataset.

The proposal would not settle whether any particular training practice qualifies as fair use. But it would give creators more information about whether their work helped train an AI system, enabling them to pursue appropriate compensation or other remedies when they believe their rights have been violated.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That kind of targeted reform offers a useful model for copyright enforcement in the age of AI. Rather than treating licensing as an obstacle to innovation, policymakers should foster a market where AI developers can efficiently license copyrighted material while respecting creators' rights.

AI innovation is vital to America's future. But America's creative industries still depend on strong copyright protections. Policymakers need to promote both.

item.title: Zelenskyy says Russia strikes hometown, criticizes Putin-Trump meeting
item.description: Zelenskyy says a Russian strike on his hometown Kryvyi Rih killed two people, including 7-year-old Tykhon, and wounded 58 others in a civilian area.
item.content:encoded:
A Russian strike on Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown, Kryvyi Rih, killed two people and wounded 58 others, the Ukrainian leader said Saturday.

A 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman were killed in the attack Friday night in the central Ukraine town, according to Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration.

Zelenkskyy said in a social media post the woman was an emergency medical worker and the boy was named Tykhon.

PUTIN LAUNCHES UKRAINE BARRAGE HOURS AFTER TRUMP MEETING AMID ALLEGED RUSSIAN MISSILE BREACH OF NATO AIRSPACE

"He was born in 2019, and, sadly, most of his life was lived during a war like this. And the Russians took his life with their strike. My condolences to their families and loved ones," Zelenkskyy said.

On top of the civilian deaths and injuries, the strike sparked four fires and damaged roughly 25 apartment buildings, along with a hospital, schools, an industrial facility, businesses and vehicles.

RUSSIA'S PUTIN VOWS A RESPONSE 'FAR MORE PAINFUL' AFTER UKRAINE ATTACKS PRIZED BRIDGE IN CRIMEA

Zelenkskyy claimed that the Russian strike hit an area of the city with no military targets.

"The strike hit an ordinary civilian area of the city – there are no military facilities nearby, and there never have been," he wrote, adding, "Russia is waging war against life, and there can be NO justification for this."

TRUMP WILL FACE REPORTERS AFTER HISTORIC XI-PUTIN TALKS AS WAR QUESTIONS LINGER

The Ukrainian leader later commented on President Donald Trump's recent trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"Putin didn't get his 'Yalta 2,'" Zelenskyy wrote, referring to the famed 1945 Yalta Conference between former U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, and Soviet Premier Joseph Stalin.

TRUMP’S PROPOSED RUSSIA DEAL RAISES NATO ALARM AS EX-COMMANDER WARNS PUTIN SEEKS INFLUENCE OVER EUROPE

"As far as I understand, he recently commented: 'What's wrong with Yalta? Those were the victories over Nazism, over fascism, and so on, that were sealed there.' First of all, indeed, this was no Yalta. Did Putin want a real Yalta? Yes. In the sense of carving up the world and changing borders. China didn't let itself be drawn into it. I don't know what happened between the United States and Russia in their bilateral, but Ukraine wasn't discussed. Nothing came out publicly. So the redrawing of borders didn't happen," Zelenskyy wrote.

"If there really was an intention to reaffirm the victory over fascism now, then the participants at this summit would have to be the United States, Europe, and Ukraine. Definitely not Russia. I think this trilateral summit turned out very badly for Russia. Not only did Putin fail to get the results he wanted, but we also saw his reaction.

"And, unfortunately, we saw that reaction in Ukraine. There was a massive attack that night – 111 missiles. If Putin wanted to remind the world once again who he is, there was no need – we haven't forgotten that he's a terrorist and a killer," his X post continued.

UKRAINE HITS PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE IN RECORD DRONE BLITZ AS KREMLIN TELLS LAWMAKERS TO PREPARE FOR 'VICTORY'

The strike on Zelenskyy's hometown is far from uncommon, with periodic Russian attacks targeting the industrial steel town dozens of times since the start of the war in 2022.

The incident also occurred as a Russian ship was struck by drones on Saturday, causing it to catch fire in the Gulf of Finland.

The Russian-flagged Sparta II was struck by a drone shortly before 9 a.m. local time, according to Finnish Coast Guard Commander Mikko Simola.

"Generally it should be noted that it is known that this Sparta II vessel has been used for transports for the Russian state, including the armed forces," Simola said.

As a result of its damage, the craft entered Finnish territorial waters. Simola also noted that Finland believed a Russian helicopter crossed Finland's sovereign borders as well.

Finnish officials believe that Ukraine was behind the attack.

"It is likely that Ukraine ... is behind (the attack)," Finnish armed forces spokesperson Aki-Mauri Huhtinen said.

Reuters contributed to this report.

item.title: Maher calls out 'spoiled brats' who left US over Trump presidency, says country ‘self-corrected’ in midterms
item.description: Bill Maher mocked the "spoiled brats" who fled to England or Ireland over Trump, questioning the patriotism of stars who left after losing elections.
item.content:encoded:
Bill Maher, host of HBO's "Real Time," took a swipe at liberals who fled the country over President Donald Trump’s administration, calling them "spoiled brats" as he celebrated Democrats’ sweep in this month’s midterm elections.

Speaking to the audience during the show’s season finale Friday night, Maher blasted Democrats who moved abroad following Trump’s election victories in 2016 and 2024.

"But it is also important to remember to mock and ridicule the spoiled brats who fled to England or Ireland because America was so irredeemably ‘Trumpian-Republican,’" Maher said as he flashed a news headline highlighting "21 celebs who fled the U.S. amid Trump’s presidency."

AMERICANS WHO MOVED TO EUROPE AFTER TRUMP WIN NOW SAY THEY REGRET LEAVING

"Only to come back to America now because America did what America does: self-corrected," he added.

Maher went on to question the judgment of those who left their country over election results that they were unhappy with, as he touted Democrats’ historic sweep in the midterm election earlier this month.

NEW YORK TIMES GLEEFUL OVER DEMOCRATS' HUGE MIDTERM VICTORIES, SAYS IT'S TIME TO ‘FEEL PRIDE’

"You left the country you're supposed to love forever because you lost an election or two, and now you look like the husband who leaves his wife because she let herself go for a while," Maher added. "Well, guess what? We got hot again."

Maher began by making fun of conservatives who left blue states: "Let's all allow ourselves a good laugh at the people who uprooted their whole lives in blue states to move to red states that are now blue states." 

He praised the results of the midterms, noting, "We should all have a little more faith that democracy can still do its thing. And it's a beautiful thing. The sound of a country turning the page, catching up with its own ideals." 

The HBO host's comments come after several high-profile celebrities — including comedians Rosie O’Donnell and Ellen DeGeneres — cited Trump’s election victory as their driving force for moving abroad.

ROSIE O'DONNELL HAMMERS TRUMP REPEATEDLY IN KIMMEL GUEST-HOST GIG AS WHITE HOUSE FIRES BACK

"We got here the day before the election and woke up to lots of texts from our friends with crying emojis, and I was like, 'He got in,'" DeGeneres told broadcaster Richard Bacon after she and her wife, Portia de Rossi, decided to relocate to the United Kingdom, according to the BBC in 2025. "And we're like, 'We're staying here.'"

O’Donnell referred to Trump as "Mango Mussolini" on the Aug. 17 episode of "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" during a week-long guest-hosting stint that brought the 64-year-old comic back to the United States from her new home in Ireland.

ART GARFUNKEL JOINS GROWING LIST OF CELEBRITIES CONSIDERING A MOVE ABROAD OVER TRUMP PRESIDENCY

"I read that Project 2025 and said, ‘Got to get myself out of here, you know,’ and I decided to go to Ireland, a place where people are driven to drink regardless of who's running their country," O’Donnell said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Musician Art Garfunkel also weighed the possibility of leaving the United States over Trump’s presidency, telling The Guardian earlier this year that he is unhappy with the administration’s handling of climate change, international affairs and other political issues.

"I don’t like America’s position at all," he told the outlet. "I’m not on board, and I’m thinking of leaving the country, frankly."

Maher's comments were noticed by Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff, who suggested to Fox News Digital that the comedian could be acting a bit hypocritical in his final monologue of the season.

"This Ireland shot is obviously a Rosie O’Donnell dig, and Maher is flattening 20 years of context to make it work," Shroff said. "Trump has singled her out since 2006 and, after she left, publicly threatened to take away her citizenship."

"You can call her decision dramatic, but it was not some celebrity tantrum over losing an election," he added. "And Maher, who can barely tolerate criticism directed at himself, is an especially funny person to lecture somebody else about having thicker skin."

NewsBusters managing editor Curtis Houck told Fox News Digital: "Bill Maher will sadly be on an island when it comes to calling out people on his own team who fled the country." 

"Anyone returning to America as though their tantrums never happened shouldn’t be taken seriously," he added. 

Fox News Digital reached out to representatives of DeGeneres and O’Donnell for comment.

item.title: Voters want to 'move on' from the president, former Trump official claims as reason for GOP's midterm defeat
item.description: Former Kansas Republican Sen. Sam Brownback says voters rejected President Trump himself, not his policies, citing inflation and gas prices.
item.content:encoded:
Former Kansas Republican Sen. Sam Brownback, who served as an ambassador during Donald Trump's first term, blamed the president's personal leadership style for Republicans' midterm losses.

He claims the outcome of the 2026 elections — where Democrats' sweeping victories in traditional red strongholds helped them reclaim majorities in the House and Senate — was a sign of voters rejecting Trump more than rebuking his policies.

"I think the thing we're missing is that it was really targeted at President Trump. I don't think it was targeted at the policies so much," Brownback told Fox News Digital in an interview. "Pride comes before a fall and a haughty spirit before a stumble."

REPUBLICANS TURN ON TRUMP AFTER DEVASTATING MIDTERM LOSSES HAND DEMOCRATS CONTROL OF CONGRESS

The former Kansas governor argued that Republicans should not write off the midterm results as the typical losses suffered by a president’s party through history during their second term.

Brownback, who represented Kansas in the U.S. Senate from 1996 to 2011 before serving as governor from 2011 to 2018, said economic concerns, including inflation and gas prices, played a role in the election results.

He suggested voters' frustrations extended beyond the economy to Trump's approach to governing.

The Fox News Voter Poll found that 89% of voters considered the cost of living a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote, compared with 74% who said the same about the war in Iran. The findings suggest broader economic frustrations were also a major concern among voters, although the two issues may overlap and the polling does not establish which ultimately drove Republican defections.

DEMS SEIZE ON MIDTERM ROUT TO DEMAND ICE REFORM, BUT POLLS REVEAL A TWIST IN WHO PRIORITIZED IMMIGRATION

"People just saying I'm ready to move on past President Trump," Brownback said, adding that voters still appreciated the administration's efforts to secure the border but viewed interior immigration enforcement as too aggressive.

The former ambassador-at-large for international religious freedom also urged Republicans to reconsider how they communicate with voters, emphasizing the importance of humility and kindness.

"You just can't be proud. You've got to come forward humbly," Brownback said. "And I think you have to do that with the American public."

Brownback called for a more measured response to voters' concerns ahead of 2028. "We hear you, American public. We're adjusting to the message that we heard," he said.

REPUBLICANS NEED HISTORY LESSON ABOUT THEIR PARTY IF THEY WANT TO MOVE ON FROM DEFEAT

"America is great because it's good. If it ever loses its goodness, it will lose its greatness," he added. "There has to be, as I keep doubling back to, a humility and a kindness about it as well."

Both Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have been floated as potential contenders for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination, with Vance saying he plans to decide whether to launch a White House bid in the spring.

item.title: Trump says Sen Cornyn is doing a 'tremendous disservice' by blocking Texas judicial pick
item.description: President Donald Trump says Sen. John Cornyn is doing a "tremendous disservice" by blocking DOJ lawyer Elliot Gaiser's federal judge nomination in Dallas.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump told Fox News' "Saturday in America" that outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn is doing a "tremendous disservice" by blocking his pick to fill a judicial seat in Dallas.

The president said, "We're going to have a radical left lunatic get in there and we don't want that."

Trump's comments come after Cornyn told The Associated Press he has no intention of returning the "blue slip" for T. Elliot Gaiser, a Department of Justice senior lawyer who was nominated by the president to the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas.

The blue slip tradition allows for home state senators to weigh in on judicial nominees, giving them a say on who does and doesn’t move forward. Returning a blue slip is the equivalent of giving a thumbs up to the nominees moving forward, while keeping the slip effectively blocks the process.

"Everybody tells me he's outstanding and he's being held up by John Cornyn because John Cornyn's feelings were hurt," said Trump, who endorsed Cornyn's challenger Ken Paxton in the Texas Republican Senate primary.

TRUMP TAKES AIM AT SENATE 'BLUE SLIP' TRADITION AS GOP RESISTS CHANGE

"And by the way, John Cornyn would have lost. It was just a point in time. John Cornyn would have lost by a lot. You know, one of those things. But he was beaten in the primary. And he's - he feels badly about it," the president continued.

"He's a nice guy, John Cornyn, but he's doing a tremendous disservice because Gaiser is fantastic," Trump added.

Cornyn wrote on X later Saturday, "If President Trump wanted to fill a judicial vacancy in Dallas, why did he wait until after the midterms to nominate someone?

"The seat has been vacant since 2025. Then, without any consultation, he nominates a non-Texan with little connection to the Lone Star State, with no trial court experience, and who has not been appropriately vetted for a lifetime job. The Senate has a constitutional responsibility to provide 'advise and consent,' which is impossible without consultation," Cornyn added.

"Still, I would like to work with the President to fill the seat while we still have a Senate majority. I have forwarded an outstanding candidate who was highly rated by Senator Cruz's and my bipartisan Federal Judicial Evaluation Committee, and who has now been interviewed by White House Counsel. All that is needed is an FBI background check with they stand ready to do on a timely basis," Cornyn also said. "Back to you, Mr. President. Time is of the essence."

CORNYN MEETS WITH SEN-ELECT TALARICO, DESCRIBES HIM AS 'BASICALLY ... A GOOD PERSON'

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, called Cornyn's move "really frustrating," describing to Fox News' "Saturday in America" a tense encounter he had with Cornyn this week in Washington.

"I came to him on the Senate floor, and I asked him to please let this judge go. And I tried to make the case on the merits that he'd make a fantastic judge. And I asked him, 'Will you just meet with him?' Because Cornyn refused even to meet with him," Cruz said.

"He wouldn't talk to him. He just said, 'no, no, no.' And I was asking him, I said, 'Look, you're going to give this seat to the Democrats. Why would you want to do that?' And unfortunately, he got very angry. He began screaming. He began cursing at me," Cruz added.

Cruz said, following the Republican losses in the midterm elections, "all the Republicans agreed, let's do everything humanly possible to confirm every judge we can before the end of the year, because we know the Democrats are going to come in January, and I expect they're going to block all judicial confirmations."

TRUMP'S SUPREME COURT MAJORITY FACES LOOMING THREAT AFTER DEM SENATE TAKEOVER: 'STUCK'

"We had two vacancies in Texas, one in Austin that we're moving forward with. And we'll have that judge confirmed by the end of the year. We had a second vacancy in Dallas, and the problem was that we did not have time to have a brand new nominee go through the paperwork, the FBI background check," Cruz told Fox News. "That takes weeks and weeks and weeks, and we simply didn't have time between now and the end of the year to get that done. And so the White House proposed a different idea, which is to go with a senior lawyer at the Department of Justice, a man named Eliot Gaiser, an incredibly qualified judicial nominee.

"This is someone who was a law clerk at the U.S. Supreme Court for Justice Sam Alito. He was a state solicitor general arguing cases before the United States Supreme Court," Cruz said. "And he's right now the head of the Office of Legal Counsel, which is the senior constitutional advisor to the president and the senior constitutional advisor to the attorney general."

Cruz also told Fox News he interviewed Gaiser and called him "incredibly principled, smart, capable, ready."

Cruz added, Gaiser "was a fantastic nomination. I was enthusiastic. Unfortunately, my colleague John Cornyn decided to block the nomination and any one senator can block a district court nomination from your state.

"And so Cornyn did what's called — he refused to return the blue slip, which basically means he vetoed it — and the result of that is the seat is going to remain vacant. The people of Dallas are not going to have a judge in that seat. And he basically gave the seat to the Democrats," Cruz said.

Fox News Digital's Alex Miller contributed to this report.

item.title: Friday night's win over Duke didn't prove Dabo Swinney is safe at Clemson, it did the opposite
item.description: Dabo Swinney's 20-10 win over Duke may have sealed his Clemson Tigers fate, echoing Jimbo Fisher and Billy Napier's late exits from college football.
item.content:encoded:
The discussions surrounding Dabo Swinney's job security as the head coach of the Clemson Tigers have reached a fever pitch.

The two-time national championship winner has fallen on hard times recently, going from perennial College Football Playoff contender to ACC also-ran.

Things appeared to have bottomed out this season, as the Tigers limped into their Friday night showdown with Duke holding a 6-4 record and having little offense to speak of in 2026.

DABO SWINNEY REACTS AFTER CLEMSON HITS LATEST LOW WITH UPSET LOSS TO GEORGIA TECH: 'NOBODY COMING TO SAVE US'

The noise regarding Dabo and his future at Clemson was only getting louder, but, miraculously, the Tigers took care of business and beat the Blue Devils 20-10 on the road.

You would think this data point would show Swinney is looking to end this season on a high note and head into 2027 with some momentum and that maybe this was his first step towards saving his job.

DABO SWINNEY SHOULD EMBRACE HIS VILLAIN ERA TO SAVE CLEMSON FOOTBALL, AFTER PROMISING NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP

You would be wrong. For multiple reasons, in fact.

Let's start with what got Dabo in this predicament in the first place.

TRANSFER PORTAL, NOT NIL, REASON FOR PARITY, CLAIMS COLLEGE FOOTBALL EXPERT BROOKS AUSTIN

Swinney's reluctance to lean into the transfer portal to supplement his roster as the rest of his conference - and the country - adapted around him will go down as one of the biggest self-made missteps in recent college football history.

That isn't news to anyone who has been following the sport for the past several years (or to anyone who has read any of my articles on the guy).

What you may find shocking is this win over Duke may actually be a sign that Dabo is all but officially done at Clemson.

Much like a dying dog who gets a last burst of energy before taking a turn, it's quite common for lame duck head coaches to go out and get one last big win before exiting stage left.

These kinds of things happen all the time, especially in power conferences with high-profile coaches.

Last year, Billy Napier was surely on his way out of Gainesville when his 1-3 Florida Gators took down a top-ten Texas team in The Swamp.

JAMES MADISON COACH BILLY NAPIER CONTINUES SELF PITY TOUR, REFUSES TO TAKE ACCOUNTABILITY FOR PAST FAILURES

That saved his job for approximately two weeks, and he was fired heading into their bye week.

Jimbo Fisher was famously fired following a blowout win over Mississippi State in 2023, holding the same 6-4 record that Clemson had heading into its game Friday night.

The fact that he won a championship at Clemson doesn't change the calculus for Dabo either.

Larry Coker won a national title in 2001 at Miami, a team many consider the greatest of all time, but five years later he was fired after a win over a top-20 Boston College squad granted the Hurricanes bowl eligibility late in the season.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Winning a football game can sometimes signify that a program is heading in the right direction, or, at the very least, that a coach has temporarily stopped the bleeding.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

For Clemson, the problems with the offense are still present, even with their ten-point fourth quarter "outburst."

item.title: Thousands of bags were stuck at airports as passengers urged to track luggage, pack lighter
item.description: Travel experts say AirTag luggage tracker and airline app alerts can protect checked bags after the Federal Aviation Administration halted flights nationwide recently.
item.content:encoded:
Travelers whose flights were disrupted by last week's nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop faced another headache once they finally landed. They didn't know if their checked bags made it to their destination.

At Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas, for instance, hundreds of unclaimed bags remained in the terminal Monday after the Friday ground stop halted air travel across the U.S. for more than four hours, the Austin American-Statesman reported. 

Airport officials say excess baggage is common after widespread flight disruptions, as airlines work to reunite travelers with their belongings.

20,000 BAGS STRANDED AFTER TECHNICAL ISSUE AT MAJOR AIRPORT LEAVES TRAVELERS SCRAMBLING

But travel experts said there are several things people can do to reduce the risk of luggage mix-ups and prepare in case it does happen, especially during the busy holiday travel season.

If your checked bag doesn't arrive, checking an airline's app is a smart first step, Florida-based travel advisor Whytney Rawls told Fox News Digital. She recommended downloading the apps for airlines you fly and turning on notifications so you can follow updates and contact the carrier through the app.

"It will help you keep everything organized and in order, especially if something goes wrong because they’re going to send the updates to that app," said Rawls, founder of The Amara Escapes and an advisor with Fora Travel. 

Rawls also suggested keeping baggage claim receipts and tag information handy. 

Take photos of the receipts and tags, too, she said, so identifying details are easy to find if a bag goes missing.

US WARNS AMERICANS IN KEY LOCATIONS TO 'KEEP A LOW PROFILE' AHEAD OF CROWDED HOLIDAY TRAVEL

A luggage tracker such as an AirTag can also help travelers see where their bags are, she said.

"That is really important," Rawls said. She suggested using one in each bag.

For those who check luggage, she said it's wise to pack as much clothing as possible in the carry-on, using vacuum-sealed bags to save space and wearing bulky items such as boots or a jacket, even when departing from a warm-weather destination, to free up space in the bag. 

"That'll get you much more space for things that you need to travel with on the plane," she said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Get travel-size toiletries," she also said.  

Taking extra precautions is especially key when connecting flights are involved, Rawls noted.

Cheryl Nelson, a Virginia-based FEMA-certified natural disaster and travel preparedness expert and founder of Prepare With Cher, recently experienced how quickly a routine trip can turn into an overnight stay. 

Delayed while trying to fly from San Francisco, she missed her Atlanta connection to Norfolk by five minutes and spent the night near the airport without her checked bag. 

Her luggage arrived the next morning.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

"I like to tell people to think of your carry-on as your insurance policy for a disrupted travel day," Nelson told Fox News Digital.

She recommended keeping medications, glasses, valuables, electronics and chargers, basic toiletries, snacks and a change of clothes with you. 

"Don’t pack something in your checked bag that you absolutely need or couldn’t easily replace," she said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Before checking a suitcase, Nelson advised removing old airline tags to limit any confusion about where the bag is headed and adding a distinctive tag or ribbon to identify common-looking luggage.

She also recommended allowing extra time for connections when possible. 

Tight layovers leave little margin for delays, gate changes or long taxi times, she said.

"Travel preparedness isn’t about expecting everything to go wrong," Nelson said. 

"It’s about having a few things with you that make a stressful situation a whole lot easier when it does."

Jessica Mekles of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

item.title: Bo Derek stands by falling for married John Derek at 16 despite 30-year age gap: 'It all worked out'
item.description: Bo Derek reflects on meeting married director John Derek at 16, while "Dynasty" star Linda Evans recalls the devastation of losing him on a Greek film set.
item.content:encoded:
Bo Derek believes "it all worked out" when it comes to her marriage to John Derek — the director who was 46 and married when she met him as a 16-year-old up-and-coming actress.

She spoke about their relationship — as did John's former wife, "Dynasty" star Linda Evans — in a new profile for The Hollywood Reporter.

John, best known for appearing alongside Charlton Heston in "The Ten Commandments," had shifted into filmmaking later in his career, and in the early 1970s, he'd set out to cast a movie he'd written titled "Fantasies" about a relationship between a teenage girl and her adoptive brother.

CAMERON MATHISON SAYS HE HAS ‘TONS’ IN COMMON WITH NEW GIRLFRIEND TAELYR ROBINSON DESPITE 24-YEAR AGE GAP

Bo, who went by her birth name, Mary Cathleen Collins, at the time, auditioned and was given the part. The film was shot in Greece, but John asked Evans to give Bo acting lessons before they departed.

As Evans recalled, Bo was "beautifully independent," and she had "zero, zero, zero" suspicions that anything romantic might develop between the teen and her then-husband.

Bo herself told the outlet that her relationship with John and the age gap they shared is "not the natural way of things," admitting, "If it were my daughter, I would have kidnapped her and taken her away from him, of course."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

She added, "At the same time, I was with him 25 years until he died. He was a very ridiculously honest, good man. And it all worked out, didn’t it?"

It was 1973 when Bo left with John for Europe to shoot the film. A few weeks later, Evans traveled to visit John on the set, which was when she'd learned that he'd fallen for Bo.

"To say I was devastated is an understatement," she said, but she maintained that Bo wasn't to blame for what happened.

AGELESS 'DYNASTY' STAR LINDA EVANS SHARES PLANS FOR 2025 IN INSPIRING NEW YEAR'S MESSAGE

"She didn’t break up my marriage," she insisted. "She did not go after him — he went after her."

THR wrote that Evans "doesn't hold much resentment for John, either," with the actress saying, "When he loved you, he was consumed with you."

She later added, "It was a favor they both did to me, because I ended up having an extraordinary life going off on my own."

And Bo, as she said, went on to have a long relationship with John that only ended when he died in 1998.

In a 1980 interview with the Washington Post, John said, "I had everything I wanted in Linda, so why I became interested in Bo I don't know. At that time she couldn't hold a candle to Linda, but something about her got me involved. She's an interesting girl, Bo is."

BO DEREK REVEALS WHY SHE FELT LIKE AN 'IMPOSTOR' AND WALKED AWAY FROM HOLLYWOOD DESPITE BLOCKBUSTER FAME

He said at the time that he was on good terms with Evans, and that she was the one who researched the legalities of returning to the U.S. with Bo – after wrapping up the film in Greece, they stayed in Germany for some time, because, as he explained, "In the United States you have statutory rape and the Mann Act to contend with."

"It was definitely more acceptable there," Bo admitted to The Hollywood Reporter.

They were married in Las Vegas in 1976, and three years later, "10" was released and Bo became an international sex symbol.

However, she wasn't quite sure she was cut out for the job.

"I remember sobbing and saying, ‘I’m so confused. I don’t know what to do,’" Bo told THR. "And my husband said, ‘Well, do what you want. Just because everybody would kill for this career doesn’t mean you have to love it.’"

She recalled telling him, "I just want to go make little films like we were doing before," referring to "Fantasies," which was finally released in 1981. She then starred in "Tarzan, The Ape Man," which John directed, as well as a couple of other films, also helmed by her husband.

Since then, she's done smaller roles here and there, saying, "I didn’t always make the right career moves. But God, it was fun."

In 2002, four years after John's death, she was set up on a date with actor John Corbett, known for his roles in "Sex and the City" and "My Big Fat Greek Wedding." The two hit it off, and as Corbett told The Hollywood Reporter, "We’ve kind of never been apart since then, really."

Bo married John in 2020, and when she was asked why they've worked so well together, she answered, "I fall in love. I fall hard, and I think that when someone else truly loves you, it’s such a gift to cherish. It’s kind of a miracle with all the billions of people in the world, so I cherish it."

item.title: Mike Waltz warns Kremlin faces 'unsustainable' losses approaching WWII scale as Trump seeks deal
item.description: United Nations Ambassador Mike Waltz says Russia is losing up to 35,000 troops a month in Ukraine, calling the battlefield losses "unsustainable."
item.content:encoded:
U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz warned Friday that Russia is suffering "unsustainable" battlefield losses, with monthly deaths outpacing recruitment numbers.

Speaking on "The Brian Kilmeade Show" podcast, Waltz echoed President Donald Trump's assessment that Russian President Vladimir Putin is "worn down," arguing the war in Ukraine cannot be won militarily and must end at the negotiating table.

"Right now, the numbers that we have, the Russians are recruiting 20,000 to 25,000 a month of new fresh recruits," Waltz said. "They're losing 30,000 to 35,000 a month, dead every single month."

TRUMP CLAIMS STUNNING CASUALTY NUMBERS IN RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR

"That is exponentially more than they lost in Afghanistan and approaching what they lost in World War II, a thousand a day," he added. "It's just unsustainable."

The interview followed Trump's return from Shenzhen, China, where he met with Putin before joining the Russian leader and Chinese President Xi Jinping for the first-ever three-way summit between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China.

CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO

The summit produced a joint declaration pledging dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, maintaining stable energy supplies and reforming the United Nations, but the leaders stopped short of announcing breakthroughs on Ukraine or Iran.

At a White House news conference Friday, Trump addressed questions about Putin's intent regarding the war.

ZELENSKYY PRESSES US FOR EXPANDED RUSSIA TALKS AS KUSHNER ANNOUNCES BREAKTHROUGH

"He'd love to end the war. It's a very hard thing to do," Trump said Friday. "To be honest, you have two guys that don't know how to end it. We're trying to help them."

"You have two people that hate each other, Zelenskyy and Putin. They don't know how to end it. They want to end it. They're both stuck in it," he added. "And it's a horrible war, actually. And I thought it would have been maybe one of the easier ones to get ended. But the personalities play."

KUSHNER ENTERS UKRAINE PEACE TALKS AS TRUMP EYES SECURING SAFEGUARDS AGAINST ANOTHER RUSSIAN INVASION

Waltz argued that both Ukraine and Russia have "worn each other down," saying it's unlikely the two countries will be able to sustain the current level of fighting.

"It's a horrific war, and the president remains determined to find some construct of a deal that will end it because neither side can sustain this war of attrition," Waltz said. "There is no winning it militarily. It's got to end diplomatically."

Fox News Digital’s Morgan Phillips contributed to this report.

item.title: High school football’s latest circus involves two brothers in Ohio, two Dodges and a $360K house
item.description: The Feister brothers were cleared for Massillon hours before kickoff as OHSAA probes recruiting questions tied to cash purchases of a house and vehicles.
item.content:encoded:
The ugly side of high school football reared its ugly head in Ohio this week, and it didn't take place on the field.

Instead, it took place in court. That's where the really ugly stuff happens, right? It's never on the field. It's always — always — in the courts.

For those who missed it, two brothers on a powerhouse Ohio football team were ruled eligible, and then ineligible, and then eligible again, for Friday night's playoff showdown. Massillon Washington football stars Brayton and Brydon Feister were allowed to play at the last minute for last night's D-II regional final game against Bishop Watterson.

HIGH SCHOOL FOOTBALL DRAMA INCLUDES A FORFEIT AND RESIGNATION, AIKMAN HATES BUCK & IS THE MLB SEASON TOAST?

Massillon lost, 22-5. The season is over. But that's not the point.

Should these two brothers — one committed to Oregon and the other with a pile of D-1 offers — have been allowed to play at all?

That's the question the state of Ohio had been grappling with all week, and it's a situation that's all too familiar to anyone who's ever dipped their toe into the world of high school football.

Context is obviously important here, so I'll try to summarize this situation the best I can ...

The Feisters transferred to Massillon last spring after spending last year at Akron's Archbishop Hoban High School.

According to Ohio High School Athletic Association (OHSAA) court filings, the move followed a disciplinary dispute at Hoban stemming from the state wrestling tournament in March.

According to OHSAA, the family refused to complete the disciplinary consequences and promptly relocated to Massillon a month later. OHSAA attorney Joseph Fraley also wrote that the family had been in contact with multiple schools about potential enrollment.

Still with me?

In Ohio, transferring athletes generally must sit out the second half of the season and the playoffs unless they qualify for an exception. One covers a legitimate family relocation, but the OHSAA must determine that the move created the need to transfer.

You also must also fill out documents to prove it wasn't for athletic reasons.

COURT RULING OPENS DOOR FOR MICHIGAN TO ADD FORMER MIAMI, BOISE STATE PLAYER TO ROSTER MID-SEASON IN WILD MOVE

That's where things get ... blurry. Again, this is nothing new. I grew up during a time down here in Florida in which you couldn't just switch schools willy-nilly. You played where you were zoned. If you wanted to play for a certain school, you had to live in that zone.

Anyway, this led to months of court battles trying to determine if the brothers would be allowed to play for Massillon this season. At first, they were denied. Then a Court of Appeals issued an injunction on Oct. 16, allowing them to play the rest of the season ...

Until Thursday, when OHSAA suspended both brothers for up to 30 days while it investigated possible recruiting violations. That's where this story takes a really nasty turn. This suspension was a separate recruiting investigation.

According to the Canton Repository, it had to do with three separate purchases worth hundreds of thousands of dollars, along with recruiting questions. A source told the Repository the family had been asked to provide documentation to explain apparent cash purchases of their Massillon house and two vehicles.

Public records show the family purchased a $360,000 house in Massillon without a mortgage being recorded. They also show the family bought a $238,655 residence in Green, Ohio last year, and took out a mortgage for $226,722. It has not yet been paid off, according to public records.

The two other purchases included a Dodge Charger and Dodge Durango. The investigation has not yet produced a final finding that the family received improper benefits.

NFL TO NCAA? COURTROOM CHAOS IS GIVING PRO ATHLETES A BIZARRE PATH BACK TO COLLEGE, AND IT'S ONLY JUST BEGUN

On Friday, Bo Feister, the boys' father, told News 5 that the family submitted 18 rounds of information to OHSAA, including deeds, titles, and bank statements. He also accused the association of harassing his family.

In a Nov. 5 Facebook post, Feister accused someone in a black truck of "following" his family, and claimed the person was operating under OHSAA direction.

"Our family is devastated. Our children are terrified. And frankly, we never imagined we would find ourselves in a position where we would have to publicly beg our own community for help protecting our children," Feister wrote.

Hours before Friday's playoff game, an appeals court reaffirmed its earlier order allowing the brothers to play and ordered the OHSAA to explain why it should not be held in contempt.

Whew. We all caught up now? What a saga.

Here's the sad part: this is nothing new for high school football. That's the reality. There's a reason a little show called "Friday Night Lights" was so popular back in the day.

School districts vs. parents. Alleged recruiting violations. Eligibility questions. Court battles. Injunctions and appeals. It's been around forever.

I grew up in a high school football world, long before this (horrible) NIL and transfer world we're currently in. There was a huge story years ago in my town about a kid playing for a school, but not actually living in the town. If I remember correctly, he lived two counties over, but his aunt had a house here and he was allegedly living with her.

You get the gist.

Stuff like that happened all the time growing up. It's been going on for years. I'm not saying that's what happened in Ohio, because I don't know. Obviously, OHSAA has some serious questions for the family. The family, obviously, pushed back — hard. A court agreed with them, at least for now.

This is the dark side of sports. The one we don't want to see. The one we know exists, but choose to ignore because, frankly, it's a huge bummer.

I love high school football. I've written about it all year. I used to cover it religiously in a previous life. I maintain that nothing beats a Friday night in a small town at a packed high school football stadium. It's the best. You don't get that feeling anywhere else.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

If you've experienced it, you know.

But I'd be lying to you if I said it hasn't lost some of its luster over the past decade or so. It certainly has down here in Florida. Rick Scott signed HB 7029 back in 2016, and it essentially paved the way for open enrollment. It was a huge deal, and a turning point for high school athletics.

It was the transfer portal before the transfer portal became a thing. Then along came NIL in college sports. And now, you basically have a local high school football team filled with star players from all over the state — some of them working out future NIL deals during the season.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

That big offensive lineman you watched throw a couple pancakes last night? He might not be from your town, and could very well be richer than you in about eight months. That's the truth.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

What does any of that have to do with the situation in Ohio this week? It's all part of the ugly side of high school athletics.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

Whether it's eligibility questions, alleged recruiting violations, potential harassment, or the corporatization of amateur athletics, it doesn't matter. It's all nasty. It's all ugly. It's all sad.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

Yes, high school sports is losing its innocence.

In reality, I'm not sure it ever really had it.

item.title: JONATHAN TURLEY: Baltimore Raven learns truth is no defense in the NFL
item.description: Ravens star Marlon Humphrey was suspended over a four-word joke about Baltimore crime on his podcast, as Mayor Brandon Scott rejected his apology.
item.content:encoded:
Baltimore Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey will not be playing this Sunday against the Carolina Panthers. He is not on the IL list, but on the FS list. Humphrey was flagged for free speech; uttering four words about the crime problem in Baltimore. The cornerback quipped that the city is "best at making criminals." While Ravens players were allowed to protest the United States at a London game, a player is not allowed to make a political comment on his personal podcast about the crime epidemic in his city. The day Humphrey was suspended, a 30-year-old woman was shot and killed near the M&T Bank Stadium. However, players would be wise not to acknowledge the crime. However, they could presumably condemn the country.

Head Coach Jesse Minter announced that Humphrey had been suspended after the 10-year veteran spoke about crime in the city on his podcast, The Marlon Humphrey Show. He was asked what Baltimore is best at making. Notably, Humphrey first offered The Star-Spangled Banner and National Bohemian beer. He then added as a joke that the city is also "best at making criminals."

Crime in Baltimore makes the city one of the most dangerous cities in the United States. Despite a drop in crime levels, it remains in the top five cities for violent crime.

WOMAN KILLED NEAR RAVENS STADIUM SAME DAY MARLON HUMPHREY SENT HOME FOR JOKE ABOUT BALTIMORE CRIMINALITY

Notably, Humphrey's comment was not only tongue-in-cheek, but was not racist or prejudiced toward any group. It was not encouraging violence or other bad conduct. On the contrary, it implied criticism of those who continue to endanger others in the city.

Yet, Minter went public with the virtue-signaling suspension.

WIFE OF RAVENS OFFENSIVE LINEMAN APOLOGIZES MULTIPLE TIMES AFTER BACKLASH FOR CALLING BALTIMORE 'SCARY'

One can only wonder whether the suspension would have happened if the Ravens were not on a dismal five-game losing streak, ranked fourth in the AFC North, and 11th in the AFC playoff rankings.

We have previously discussed how players are not entitled to protest on the field in relation to the kneeling demonstrations. The same rule applies to other employees from Starbucks to Whole Foods. Employers are allowed to limit political expression and protests in the workplace.

COLIN KAEPERNICK IS RIGHT ABOUT THE NFL'S 'PERFORMATIVE' RACISM CAMPAIGN — BUT HE'S ALSO A HYPOCRITE

Companies also may contractually subject employees to discipline for public comments or actions that bring controversy or disrepute to the company.

However, that does not make this right. I was critical of kneeling demonstrations during games, but I fully supported players' right to voice their views outside the game.

NFL RESTARTS SOCIAL JUSTICE MESSAGING WHILE BATTLING DOMESTIC ABUSE, DRUNK DRIVING AND PROSTITUTION ARRESTS

The NFL is notorious for hypocrisy and inconsistency in punishing free speech. The Humphrey controversy is reminiscent of the Commanders hammering a coach for expressing a different view of January 6.

The NFL has spent years virtue-signaling with statements on helmets and in the end zones. However, when players or coaches express opposing views, they are silenced or suspended.

NFL TOLD AZEEZ AL-SHAAIR HE'D BE PULLED FROM TEXANS GAME OVER PRO-PALESTINIAN EYEBLACK MESSAGE

The NBA is little better. LeBron James can show disrespect to the National Anthem, but Jaden Ivy was fired for expressing his opposition to Pride Month. Players are expected to engage in mandatory speech while remaining silent on their own views.

Nevertheless, Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott rejected an apology by Humphrey: "While we acknowledge Marlon’s apology, a verbal apology is not enough." He added that Baltimore is "a city full of young Black boys who look to the Ravens as a beacon of light in their lives."

TEXANS' AZEEZ AL-SHAAIR TO BE FINED ONCE AGAIN BY NFL FOR WEARING PRO-PALESTINIAN PERSONAL MESSAGE ON EYEBLACK

That is a curious objection, since Humphrey was highlighting the failure of Scott to make the city safe to protect those lives, given its top-five ranking for criminal violence.

The message is clear. Players are expected to wear and repeat approved views of the team. For the NFL, speech codes reflect whatever values are popular or approved by NFL commissioner Roger Goodell and team owners.

CARDINALS BACKUP CORNERBACK FINED BY NFL FOR WRITING 'GLORY BE 2 GOD' ON HIS EYEBLACK

Now players are on notice that they cannot comment on blue cities being breeding grounds for crime. It is a curious sensitivity for a sport that often sounds like a gangbanger's delight from shotgun and pistol formations.

The NFL and teams should get out of the speech regulation business and focus on football. While they are private companies and not directly subject to First Amendment limits, that does not mean that there are no free speech values at issue in these controversies.

JONATHAN TURLEY: FRANCE'S FREE SPEECH CRACKDOWN SHOWS WHAT HAPPENS WHEN POLITICIANS DEFINE TRUTH

The First Amendment is not the full or exclusive embodiment of free speech. It addresses just one of the dangers to free speech posed by government regulation. Many of us view free speech as a human right. Corporate censorship of social media clearly impacts free speech, and replacing Big Brother with a cadre of Little Brothers actually allows for far greater control of free expression.

Humphrey has now issued the perfunctory apology and is publicly covering himself with sackcloth and ashes. While Baltimore can no longer be called "best at making criminals," the NFL certainly remains the best in coercing silence.

It is fitting that the team was named in reference to Edgar Allan Poe’s poem "The Raven." Any effort by a player to express himself freely in Baltimore will be met by the same answer from Humphrey's attempt at free speech: "Quoth the Raven[s], ‘Nevermore.’"

item.title: Chuck Norris’ ‘Firewalker’ co-star doesn’t regret quitting Hollywood: ‘I’m glad I’m out of it’
item.description: Melody Anderson, the "Flash Gordon" star who shared the screen with Chuck Norris, reveals why she quit acting to become a therapist helping families heal.
item.content:encoded:
Melody Anderson knew when it was time to say goodbye to Hollywood.

The "Flash Gordon" star, who once shared the screen with Chuck Norris, grew tired of the uncertainty of showbiz and the constant pressure to land her next role. So she traded acting for a new calling: helping families as a therapist.

And she hasn't looked back.

DAVID CHARVET ADMITS HE WALKED AWAY FROM HOLLYWOOD AFTER 'BAYWATCH' TO FOCUS ON FATHERHOOD

"I saw the writing on the wall," the former actress, who is marking the 40th anniversary of her Norris action-adventure comedy "Firewalker," told Fox News Digital.

"Part of it was aging out," she explained. "There was also the financial insecurity of always having to wait for a job. I thought, 'I've got to start organizing my life by the time I got into my mid-30s because I realized this is not something I can count on unless I win the lottery.' I still haven't. I still buy tickets, though!"

"It wasn't really that scary for me to make that decision," Anderson continued. "The work was getting slower. My brain was getting duller. I wanted to pursue a career that would keep me growing. The curiosity and desire to learn keeps me young."

WATCH: CHUCK NORRIS DEAD AT 86

"Do I miss Hollywood? I miss being on the set. The crew was always so great. I loved the creative energy. I loved acting. But the actual business? I'm glad I'm out of it. I don't miss the business at all. There's always the anxiety of, 'When will my next job come in?' 'Will it come in time so I can pay my mortgage?' All that extra stress becomes more intense as you get older in the business."

"I am so glad I don't have to deal with that anymore," Anderson added.

Anderson stopped acting in 1995. Today, she is a licensed clinical social worker and therapist who specializes in addiction and recovery, trauma treatment and family therapy.

"When you're on a set, you hear a lot of stories from people," Anderson said. "I loved listening to people, hearing about their triumphs and struggles. I remember someone told me, 'You're pretty good at this. Have you ever thought about going back to school and getting a master's degree in social work?' I thought, 'Never.' But it really spoke to me. That's when I started working at a treatment center in New York and taking courses. I learned I loved family therapy."

"One of the reasons I love this career is because you can get really old, fat and wrinkled, and you can still help people," she said. "I've been doing this for over 30 years now, and it's just so rewarding. I work with my clients to help them find peace and some healing. It's a wonderful life to live. On my deathbed, I'll know I did a good job, not for being the greatest actress, but for wanting to help others find peace."

Still, Anderson has fond memories of her time in Hollywood, especially working opposite Norris. The actor died March 19, 2026, at 86.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"Chuck loved doing tricks on set," she said with a laugh. "He loved to tease me. I remember he had this fake poop thing, and he put it right by my chair. But I immediately identified that it was from him because I'm also a prankster. I love spiders and bugs so it takes a lot to spook me. I just thought, 'Oh my God, he thinks I'm going to fall for this?'"

"I thought, 'I'm going to tell him this is stupid,'" she recalled. "But then he was going to punish me with an even greater prank. I wanted to make sure he never knew there would be a day when I would come and get him. I was going to get back at Chuck Norris. And he wouldn't suspect a thing."

During a break from filming, Anderson came across a wooden sculpture at a local market. She had an idea.

item.title: California school board defies state by passing policy banning trans athletes from girls sports
item.description: Chino Valley Unified approved a policy barring biological males from girls sports, locker rooms and showers, defying a warning from Rob Bonta's office.
item.content:encoded:
A California school district has adopted a sweeping new policy barring biological males from girls sports, locker rooms and showers, setting up a potential legal showdown with state officials who warned the district against approving the restrictions.

The Chino Valley Unified School District Board of Education voted 4-1 Thursday to approve the policy authored by outgoing board President Sonja Shaw, despite opposition from California Attorney General Rob Bonta's office and the district's teachers union.

Shaw, who has previously clashed with California officials over parental rights and transgender student policies, said the vote marked a significant escalation in her efforts to protect female athletes and called on other school districts across the state to follow.

MICHIGAN SCHOOL BOARD VOTES TO BAN BIOLOGICAL MALES FROM GIRLS' SPORTS IN MAJOR POLICY SHIFT

"Yesterday we passed a policy I authored that went beyond statements and resolutions," Shaw told OutKick on Friday. "Last night we took it further. We passed actual board policy that establishes clear protections for girls in sports, locker rooms, showers, and overnight school travel."

"These are common-sense measures: no boys competing in girls’ sports, no boys sharing girls’ locker rooms or showers, and no boys and girls sharing hotel rooms on school trips. They protect girls’ privacy and safety in the most basic ways."

Shaw claimed Chino Valley Unified is the first California school district to formally adopt such restrictions, following a resolution she authored in 2025 that was subsequently adopted by other districts.

"We are the first district in California to put these protections into formal board policy," she said. "We have millions of children in public schools across this state, and parents should not have to wonder whether their daughters’ privacy and safety are being protected."

The policy, titled "Fairness in Girls' Athletics and Privacy in Sex-Based Facilities," establishes eligibility for girls athletic teams based on biological sex at birth rather than gender identity.

Under the accompanying administrative regulations, eligibility will generally be determined using existing student enrollment records reflecting sex at or near birth. When those records are unavailable or have been amended, the district may require a birth certificate issued around the time of birth or a statement from a licensed healthcare provider based on a routine athletic physical.

The regulations also explicitly prohibit requiring students to undergo additional examinations, tests or inspections beyond the standard physical required of all athletes.

Shaw said the changes go beyond symbolic opposition to California's existing transgender student policies.

"I authored the original resolution because someone needed to stand up and say enough. Yesterday I took that fight to the next level and gratefully our board passed it with a majority," she said. "I am sick and tired of adults pointing fingers about who is responsible and who can fix it. More districts should follow."

"The only controversy here should be that there was any opposition at all."

FEDERAL JUDGE DISMISSES DOJ LAWSUIT CHALLENGING CALIFORNIA POLICY ALLOWING BIOLOGICAL MALES IN GIRLS’ SPORTS

The vote came one day after Bonta's office sent the district a letter warning that the proposed restrictions conflicted with California law.

Deputy Attorney General Edward Nugent urged the district to reject or postpone the policy.

"Because the Proposed Policies conflict with Education Code ... the Board should reject the proposal, or at the very least, delay the vote to allow for discussion of the District’s understanding regarding the applicability of state law to the Proposed Policies," Nugent wrote in a Wednesday letter to the school system.

The law, enacted through Assembly Bill 1266 in 2013, has been a central point of conflict between California officials and the Trump administration over transgender participation in girls sports.

Shaw rejected the state's warning and publicly challenged Bonta, arguing that federal law takes precedence over conflicting state requirements.

The district's policy specifically invokes the U.S. Supreme Court's June 30 decision in West Virginia v. B.P.J. and Little v. Hecox , which upheld laws in West Virginia and Idaho restricting participation in female sports to biological females. However that ruling only protects the state laws that currently exist to protect women's sports.

In California, the state continues to maintain laws allowing transgender students to compete according to their gender identity.

In August, a federal district court dismissed the Trump administration's lawsuit against the California Department of Education and CIF over the state's transgender athlete policies. The court did not resolve the broader question of whether transgender participation in girls sports violates Title IX, instead finding insufficient legal notice to justify imposing the federal government's interpretation as a condition of funding.

The Chino Valley policy directs the superintendent to consult legal counsel and take lawful steps to protect students and federal funding if state requirements are applied in a manner that conflicts with the district's new restrictions.

The vote came during Shaw's final meeting on the Chino Valley school board after she unsuccessfully ran for California superintendent of public instruction earlier this month.

Shaw has emerged as one of California's most outspoken school board officials on parental rights and transgender student policies, previously leading efforts to require schools to notify parents about certain changes in their children's gender identification.

That policy became the subject of litigation involving Bonta's office, part of an ongoing dispute over parental notification requirements and state protections for transgender students.

In her latest statement, Shaw directly challenged California's political and educational leadership, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, Bonta, lawmakers, teachers unions and the California Department of Education.

"And let me say it once again to the teachers unions, the Attorney General, our Governor, the state legislators, and the California Department of Education, the same ones who came after me when I proposed a landmark policy to protect parents’ constitutional rights," Shaw said.

item.title: Trump says Vance, Rubio are 'doing fantastically' ahead of 2028 Republican presidential primary
item.description: Donald Trump says JD Vance and Marco Rubio are "doing fantastically" and "both very, very popular" as the 2028 Republican primary field takes shape.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump told Fox News' "Saturday in America" that JD Vance and Marco Rubio are "doing fantastically" and are "both very, very popular" when asked who he would like to see run on the Republican and Democratic tickets ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

Trump spoke highly about the vice president and secretary of state after being asked for his choices by host Kayleigh McEnany.

"Well, I think it's boiling down now. You're starting to see some people emerge. I was a little surprised to see Kamala [Harris] is doing pretty well," Trump said about his 2024 challenger and former vice president when discussing the Democrats' options.

"I think AOC [Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.] is doing well and just watching that, you know, look you could have people. And most likely, I think, at least on the Democrat side, you're going to have maybe somebody that nobody ever heard of," Trump continued. "That's a real possibility. Somebody that maybe is very good but not known.

TRUMP SIGNALS SURPRISING APPROACH TO CHOOSING HIS SUCCESSOR AS GOP'S 2028 FIELD GROWS

"On the Republican side, you know, you could have — there are quite a few people that could be very good. Obviously, JD's vice president, Marco is right up there. The two of them are doing fantastically," Trump added. "They're both very, very popular. But you could have some surprises. We have some very capable people."

In addition to Vance and Rubio, other Republicans whose names have been mentioned as possible 2028 candidates include Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, former Vice President Mike Pence, former Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp and former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin, among others.

TRUMP RESPONDS AFTER VANCE BLAMES IRAN WAR FOR MIDTERM LOSSES, VP SAYS HIS JOB IS TO SUPPORT PRESIDENT

item.title: FBI probes second cyberattack in months as hackers breach key crime database, sources say
item.description: Hackers breached the FBI's National Crime Information Center, sources say, as the bureau probes the entry point and what data was compromised.
item.content:encoded:
Hackers breached the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), three sources familiar with the matter told Fox News, marking the second cyberattack against the bureau in months.

The FBI is investigating the hack to determine the unauthorized entry point, but for now, it is unclear what information was compromised, sources said.

The NCIC database is a critical information-sharing tool for federal, state and local authorities, helping them track fugitives, monitor registered sex offenders, check whether someone has failed a gun background check, among many other things.

In an interview with Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany on Saturday morning, President Donald Trump said he had "just heard" about the hack.

TECH OUTAGE CASCADE EXPOSES US VULNERABILITIES TO FOREIGN CYBER THREATS

"I will say that it’s not good. I don’t like that," Trump added.

The FBI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. CNN first reported the hack.

In September, a group called ShinyHunters hacked into the FBI's job portal website intending to steal sensitive employment records.

The mysterious group, known for extortion plots, claimed it stole sensitive information belonging to almost every FBI agent, including names, home addresses, Social Security numbers, assignments and, in some cases, the names of family members.

FBI STRIKES BACK AT HACKING GROUP WITH OVERSEAS ARREST OF ALLEGED LEADER

Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky was arrested on Oct. 8 and faces federal extortion conspiracy charges in connection with the FBI's investigation into ShinyHunters, according to court records and law enforcement sources that spoke to Reuters.

The details of Dubrovsky's alleged crimes are unknown as the court records in relation to his case remain sealed.

FBI Director Kash Patel announced the arrest of ShinyHunters "suspected co-conspirator" on Oct. 9, a day after Dubrovsky was taken into custody.

"This is the latest arrest this FBI has made in a matter of days involving this network, as we work non-stop to dismantle the group, pursue new leads and evidence, and act quickly," Patel said in a statement at the time. "We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what’s left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate."

In 2023, hackers infiltrated a computer network at the FBI's New York field office used in child sexual exploitation cases — a system that also stored images tied to the Jeffrey Epstein probe, CNN previously reported.

item.title: History buff links prominent colonial New Yorker to notorious pirate heist
item.description: Amateur historian James Bailey says colonial records suggest Thomas Jones, the namesake of Jones Beach, helped pirate Capt. Henry Every dodge authorities.
item.content:encoded:
An amateur historian believes he's found clues suggesting a link between a notorious 17th-century pirate and the namesake of New York's famous Jones Beach — and says he has the documents to back it up.

James Bailey, who found ancient coins linked to pirate Capt. Henry Every — known as the "King of the Pirates" — in 2014, recently said colonial-era records suggest Every and his crew got an assist from Thomas Jones, the namesake of the Long Island state park, The Associated Press (AP) reported.

Bailey was metal detecting at Sweet Berry Farm, a fruit orchard in Middletown, Rhode Island, when he unearthed an Every-linked 17th-century Arabian coin over a decade ago.

TREASURE HUNTERS FIND BIGGEST VIKING COIN HOARD IN COUNTRY'S HISTORY: 'WITHOUT PARALLEL'

It wasn't until 2021 that Bailey publicized his discovery to the AP and dug deeper into colonial records — which led him to do further research on Every and Jones.

Every is best known for leading the 1695 raid on the royal Indian treasure ship Ganj-i-Sawai in the Red Sea — making off with tens of millions of dollars in gold and silver before vanishing in what some consider the first worldwide manhunt.

Bailey — whose claims are not yet independently verified — said documents suggest Jones was recruited to serve as a "wheelman" for Every and help the crew steer clear of authorities.

"You have millions of visitors and generations of New Yorkers going to this beach," Bailey told the AP.

TREASURE HUNTERS RECOVER RARE SILVER BAR FROM LEGENDARY SHIPWRECK OFF FLORIDA KEYS

"Nobody knew he was actually a major player in arguably the biggest heist in the history of piracy."

Even during his lifetime, a document showed that New York's governor investigated Jones after he had already become the proprietor of a whaling operation, AP reported.

Jones was born in Ireland and moved to Rhode Island and New York before acquiring acres of land that now comprise Jones Beach.

How exactly he made his fortune was considered a mystery both now and after his death.

REVOLUTIONARY WAR ARTIFACTS UNEARTHED AT SITE OF INFAMOUS COLONIAL AMERICAN HEIST: 'VERY SURPRISED'

In 1906, one of his descendants addressed the rumors that Jones was a pirate, calling them "slander" and "improbable fictions."

"People were disposed to cast slurs upon his memory, either for mischievousness, or a spirit of malice," the writer, Thomas Floyd-Jones, said at the time.

He added, "These myths were cherished for over a century after his death, which ignorance and superstition did not fail to magnify."

Meagan Schulman, a Fordham University doctoral candidate who specializes in 17th-century piracy and was not involved in the research, told the AP that, since Jones was already a privateer authorized to raid commercial ships of rivals, he could already be considered a pirate.

It was only when war ended that those who continued to do so were called pirates.

"The reality was that privateers were pirates, just sponsored by a certain government or patron," said Schulman, as the AP reported.

"So maybe the short answer is, yes. Jones can be called a pirate, by some people, but he probably did not ever see himself as one."

Part of Jones' wealth came when his father-in-law gifted him a lot of land — something Bailey suggests gave him a fresh start.

Richard Blakemore, a maritime history professor at the University of Reading in the United Kingdom, told the AP that Bailey's research is persuasive but not yet definitive.

He added that the records point to how deeply early British colonies were intertwined with piracy.

"Popular images of pirates show them as outcasts, but many historians have argued the opposite, based on evidence like this," Blakemore said.

item.title: 'Economic populist' Texas Gov-elect Gina Hinojosa eyes talks with Elon Musk
item.description: Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa calls herself an "economic populist" as she weighs a data center moratorium and reduced ICE cooperation in Texas.
item.content:encoded:
Texas' Democratic governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, shared details about her political philosophy as she prepares to lead the Lone Star State.

"I'd call myself an economic populist," she told "Special Report" anchor Bret Baier on Thursday. "What I heard across the state is that people want a government that is going to roll up its sleeves and deliver."

Hinojosa's self-description could be significant for Elon Musk, whose companies SpaceX and Tesla are both headquartered in Texas. Musk, who reportedly spent around $500 million on Republican candidates and causes in the midterm elections, predicted at this week's New York Times DealBook Summit that "the new governor is going to be quite moderate." 

Hinojosa told Baier that she looks forward to working with Musk.

"This is a government that people pay for," she said. "It should be working for them."

NEW TEXAS GOVERNOR-ELECT STRIKES CONCILIATORY TONE TOWARD MUSK AFTER CAMPAIGNING AGAINST SPACEX DEAL

Hinojosa is the first Democrat elected governor of Texas since Ann Richards won in 1990, a victory Hinojosa described as a "mandate for change."

The governor-elect said oneo f her first priorities is to impose a moratorium on new data center permits until new safeguards are put in place, though she doesn't expect data center companies to leave the state.

"I don't hate data centers," she told Baier. "I just hate the way they're taking advantage of Texans right now."

Hailing from the border city of Brownsville, Hinojosa said she understands Americans who want a secure border. Her agenda, however, includes reducing cooperation between Texas law enforcement and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

HOUSTON MAYOR BOLTS EARLY FROM ICE COOPERATION AFTER BLUE WAVE CRASHES IN TEXAS

"We've had people killed, Americans killed, people mowed down in the streets," she said. "That needs to end. I will not facilitate that."

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin denounced Texas officials who plan to end local law enforcement's cooperation with ICE, warning that doing so would be "of the worst derelictions of duty we've seen in a very long time."

Hinojosa said she makes a distinction between ICE and Border Patrol, saying she wants to strengthen border security through cooperation with the Trump administration, local law enforcement and Mexican counterparts.

One Democrat says he favors Hinojosa's approach and her willingness to work with the Trump administration.

"I think if the [Democratic Party] takes a hard left, this will be a short-lived majority. And I feel the same for the great state of Texas," said Rep. Vicente Gonzalez, D-Texas. "I think now that we have the power, we need to use it thoughtfully and carefully."
